doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

chapter: Nellie Lutcher and Lambert, Hendricks & Ross
title: Replacing Walter Bolden, via Les Jazz Modes and Gildo Mahones
summary: He joins after the first Columbia album is half done, recommended by Gil Mahones, whom he knew from Charlie Rouse's Les Jazz Modes.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: Yeah, but you ended up with them after their first Columbia— © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

After their Columbia album was half completed. That was after they had made their records on Verve or I forget, ABC Paramount, “Sing a Song of Basie,” “Sing Along with Basie.” “Sing a Song of Basie” was the multi-track overdubbing. “Sing a Song of Basie” was with Basie’s band but I think Nat Pierce played piano not Basie, and Joe Williams sang, and Jon Dave and Annie didn’t overdub anything they just sang along with the band I think. And then they were signed — that was such a splash, I can remember hearing them on the radio all the time before I ever knew any of them. Curiously enough Jon Hendricks came into the Five Spot a few times when I was working there from January through May of ’59 with Mal Waldron as the house rhythm section, but I didn’t know who he was, and I had heard this guy Jon Hendricks, Jon Hendricks this, Jon Hendricks — and I said who is this Jon Hendricks? And who is this guy who comes in the Five Spot all the time glad-handing everybody. Eventually I would get it. But yeah they were a big hit and they were favorites of some influential people — Hugh Hefner loved them. And we played at his festivals and I think they won the Playboy jazz polls back then and we went to his house before he moved to LA two or three times, on the north side, near the north side of Chicago. We were on his original variety talk show “Playboy’s Penthouse Party” which I think was a syndicated program. I think it came on here in New York on WOR, which is now the WB channel — no not the WB, UPN9. Well Gil Mahones recommended me. And we had worked together before that with Les Jazz Modes, a quintet that Charlie Rouse and Julius Watkins co-led. And when I first got here I can remember seeing their album covers in the window of The Bohemia, they were like, well they created some stir. They were a little novel, the saxophone and French horn with complicated arrangements. And I kept seeing and hearing about them — Le Jazz Modes — and one time at a jam session open to everybody at Count Basie’s Lounge in Harlem Charlie Rouse came up to me and asked me if I was interested in working with his group. I of course knew who Charlie Rouse was. I had had a couple of 78s with him and Fats Navarro when I was a teenager, and I was honored, I said yeah, of course. And I worked with them for, I don’t know, a couple of years, played some concerts. We played the Newport festival, that was the first time I ever played at Newport. And Gildo was the pianist. And I had heard of Gildo because there used to be broadcasts in the 50s from Birdland and you could get them on the radio in Utica, AM broadcasts. And I heard Count Basie’s band when Sonny Payne had just joined the band. To me he revolutionized the whole feel of the band. He sounded sort of like a Bebop drummer, even though when you heard him by himself in a small group he sounded like he came from an earlier era, but he made the band sound almost like Dizzy Gillespie’s big band, like a Bebop band. And I can remember hearing Lester Young’s group from Birdland as well, broadcasting, with Jesse Drakes playing trumpet and Gildo playing piano and Connie Kaye playing © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

drums, and I think John Ore was the bassist. And so I knew who Gildo was while I was still a teenager before I ever moved to New York. And then I got to meet him and we became friends. And he recommended me — he took the job with Lambert, Hendricks and Ross I guess sometime in ’58 or late ’58 maybe. And he recommended me when Walter Bolden left. And they hired me. And the first thing I did with them was I think I played a Monterey Festival. We left New York and drove all the way across country to Monterey and played that and then we came back to New York and finished that “Hottest New Group in Jazz” album, their first Columbia album. So Walter Bolden had done half and I did the other half.
